concept.name: Probability distribution
concept.definition: A mathematical function that assigns probabilities to the possible outcomes of a random variable. For discrete variables it is a probability mass function giving P(X = x) with all masses non-negative and summing to 1; for continuous variables it is a probability density function whose integral over the whole line is 1, with probabilities defined over intervals.
concept.intuition: It is the complete map of what values a random quantity can take and how likely each is - the 'shape of uncertainty' for a variable such as tomorrow's return.
concept.mechanics: A discrete PMF p(x) satisfies p(x) >= 0 and SUM p(x) = 1, with P(X = x) = p(x) at each value. A continuous PDF f(x) satisfies f(x) >= 0 and integrates to 1; the probability of any single point is zero and interval probabilities are areas under the curve. The cumulative distribution function F(x) = P(X <= x) gives left-tail probabilities in both cases.
concept.formula: Discrete: SUM_j p_j = 1, p_j >= 0. Continuous: integral_{-inf}^{+inf} f(x) dx = 1, f(x) >= 0; P(a <= X <= b) = integral_a^b f(x) dx.
concept.failure_modes: Real financial return series rarely match any simple parametric distribution exactly - they show skewness, excess kurtosis, volatility clustering, and regime changes - so a fitted distribution understates tail risk if taken literally. For continuous models, treating density height as a probability is a category error.
concept.misconceptions: A probability density is not a probability: f(x) can exceed 1, and only areas under it are probabilities. Also, knowing a distribution's mean and variance does not determine the distribution - many shapes share the same two moments.
concept.example: Modeling the number of daily limit-up moves in a year with a binomial distribution and tomorrow's percentage price change with a normal distribution are both choices of a probability distribution; each implies different tail odds.
